title: Twenty-five named prophets
hook: the Qur'an names twenty-five prophets, from Adam to Muhammad ﷺ

segments.voice: Yesterday closed al-Mursalat, and your line: don't deny it. Did you accept one good thing out loud? Today a new stretch begins: the whole book in view, gathered by theme. Day six hundred sixty-four.

For more than three hundred days this year, the path has walked the Qur'an surah by surah, from the Opening to the edge of the thirtieth part. Now it steps back. The next weeks hold the book up like a map, and trace the roads that run all the way through it. The first road is people. Open almost any surah and someone is there: a man building an ark, a boy in a well, a father on a mountain with his son. Count the prophets the Qur'an names, and you get twenty-five.

The word is nabi, a prophet. Most lexicons connect it to naba', news: a nabi is one who receives news from Allah and passes it on. Some link it to a root meaning to be raised up. Beside it stands rasul, a messenger. Many scholars explain the pair this way: every messenger is a prophet, but not every prophet was sent with a new message or law. Here are the twenty-five names. Adam. Idris. Nuh. Hud. Salih. Ibrahim. Lut. Isma'il. Ishaq. Ya'qub. Yusuf. Ayyub. Shu'ayb. Musa. Harun. Dhul-Kifl. Dawud. Sulayman. Ilyas. Al-Yasa'. Yunus. Zakariyya. Yahya. 'Isa. And Muhammad ﷺ, called the seal of the prophets in surah thirty-three. Eighteen of them appear in one passage alone, in al-An'am, chapter six, one name after another. Many will sound familiar from other scriptures: Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, John, Jesus. Hud, Salih and Shu'ayb are sent to Arabian peoples and don't appear in the Bible. And the list isn't the whole family. The Qur'an says plainly that some messengers' stories it has told, and some it has not. A report in Musnad Ahmad puts the number of prophets in the tens of thousands, though scholars debate its chain. The Qur'an also tells believers to say: we make no distinction between any of His messengers. And a hadith in al-Bukhari gives the picture behind today's line. The Prophet said the prophets are brothers with different mothers and one religion. Different times, different peoples, one family.

The practice: say all the names you know. Sit comfortably. Start at the beginning, with Adam, and say each prophet's name you can remember, quietly or in your head, slowly, one per breath. Don't worry about the order or the gaps. When you get stuck, pause on the last name and recall one thing about him: an ark, a well, a staff, a whale. Many Muslims add peace be upon him after each name; if that's yours, add it. The bell holds the time.
Nabi. A prophet, one who brings news from Allah. Twenty-five are named in the Qur'an, from Adam to Muhammad ﷺ, and more are left unnamed. Today's word.
Your line: they are one family. Today, when you hear one of these names, Noah, Moses, Jesus, Abraham, in a film, a song or a street sign, remember it's one of twenty-five. Day six hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Muslim children often learn the twenty-five prophets named in the Qur'an as a list, and Muslims add "peace be upon him" (alayhi as-salam) after each prophet's name.

fork.setup: a friend asks: how many prophets were there? what does the Qur'an itself say?
options: some it has told of, and some it has not.
fork.reveal: twenty-five are named, but the Qur'an says plainly that others were sent whose stories it doesn't tell.

original.note: Arabic: a prophet. most lexicons link it to naba', news.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prophet tells the future.
what it means: a nabi brings news from Allah; twenty-five are named in the Qur'an, as one family.
what a scholar hears: nabi and rasul: many say every rasul is a nabi, not every nabi a rasul; eighteen are named together in 6:83–86.

notes: The list of twenty-five follows the common count; some scholars discuss whether Dhul-Kifl was a prophet, and others (Luqman, Dhul-Qarnayn, 'Uzayr, al-Khidr) are mentioned but not usually counted. Confirm presentation.
Etymology of nabi (naba', news; or a root meaning elevation) as in standard lexicons; confirm.
The nabi/rasul distinction is stated as 'many scholars'; confirm wording.
Hadith numbers cited from memory (Bukhari 3443); the Musnad Ahmad report of 124,000 prophets is described as having a debated chain. Confirm.
'Tens of thousands' is used instead of the exact number in the voice; confirm acceptable.
